In Praise of Wandering: A Thousand Words on Noticing

There is a particular freedom in being told to write about anything. No topic, no thesis demanded in advance, no right answer to chase. Just an open field and an invitation to wander through it. I think most of us rarely get that anymore. Our writing — and maybe our thinking too — is so often shaped by a question someone else asked, a box to fill, a deadline to meet, a test to pass. So when someone says, just go, write freely, it feels a little like being handed a blank map and told the territory is yours to invent. For a moment I don't quite know where to start, and then all at once, I want to start everywhere.

I want to start with mornings, because mornings are the most honest draft of a day. There is a version of the world at 6 a.m. that doesn't exist at noon. The light comes in sideways, lower and more forgiving, catching dust in the air and making it look like something deliberate. The kettle takes its small eternity to boil. The street outside hasn't decided what kind of day it wants to be yet. I love that in-between feeling, when possibilities haven't narrowed. You could be anyone in a morning. You could pick up a notebook and become a person who keeps a notebook. You could go for a walk and become a person who notices birds. It's not that mornings are magical in some greeting-card sense. It's that they are quiet enough for you to hear yourself think before the world turns up the volume.

And thinking, real thinking, requires a kind of attention we are losing. Attention is my favorite subject, because everything else depends on it. What you pay attention to becomes, in a very real sense, your life. If you spend a year attending mostly to outrage and hurry and small glowing rectangles, that will be your year, no matter what else happened in the background. If you spend it attending to friends and trees and sentences and meals, that will be your year instead. Attention is not just a mental resource; it's a moral choice, an aesthetic choice, a way of voting for the kind of world you want to live in. I don't mean this in a scolding way. I get distracted constantly. My mind is a browser with thirty tabs open and one of them is playing music I can't find. But I've started to treat attention like a garden: it needs weeding, watering, fences. Put the phone in another room. Look out the window for longer than feels productive. Listen to the end of someone's sentence.

One of the best places to practice attention is in a library or a bookstore, or even just in front of your own overcrowded shelf. Books are patient in a way almost nothing else is now. They don't ping you. They don't auto-play the next chapter to keep you hooked, at least not in the same needy way. They wait. A book you bought five years ago and never opened is still there, without resentment, still holding whatever it held. I love the physical fact of books, too — the weight, the smell of paper and glue, the marginalia of strangers if you're lucky enough to find a used copy. Someone underlined a sentence in 1987 and thought, yes, this is true. And now you are holding their yes. Reading is time travel and mind meld at once. You sit still and someone dead for a hundred years starts talking directly into your head, and somehow you answer back.

If books are stillness, trains are motion that still lets you think. I have a theory that many of our best thoughts happen at about 60 miles per hour while looking out a window. There's something about being in transit — not here, not there, temporarily relieved of responsibility — that loosens the mind. Car travel is too tense, air travel is too cramped and procedural, but trains hit the sweet spot. You can walk around. You can stare. The landscape edits itself in long, slow cuts: backyards, warehouses, cows, a river appearing alongside you like it's keeping you company. Strangers read or doze or eat sandwiches wrapped in foil. Nobody expects anything from you. I have solved more problems, forgiven more people, and started more essays on trains than anywhere else. If I could prescribe anything for a stuck life, it would be: take a longer train than you need, bring no entertainment, bring a window seat and a notebook.

Conversations deserve a place in this wandering too, because they are where thinking becomes two-player. Not debates, not networking, not small talk about the weather as a way to avoid weather inside us — but real, meandering conversation. The kind that starts about groceries and ends up about grief or God or what it was like to be twelve. I love questions that have no efficient answer: What has been quietly shaping you lately? What are you hoping for that you haven't said out loud? What did you love before the world told you what to love? We don't ask each other these things enough, maybe because we're afraid of the silence that follows, or the honesty. But that silence is fertile. Good conversation is jazz, not a presentation. You riff, you miss notes, you find a melody you didn't know you knew. And afterward you feel slightly more awake, slightly more human, as if someone polished a window you didn't know was dirty.

Making things is another way of staying awake. Not necessarily art with a capital A, but the humble act of making: cooking a soup without a recipe, fixing a wobbly chair, knitting a lopsided scarf, planting basil and actually keeping it alive for once, writing a bad poem on purpose just to get the badness out. There is a satisfaction in using your hands that no amount of scrolling can replicate. The world of screens is weightless and endless; the world of things resists you, and that resistance is a gift. Dough tears if you rush it. Wood splits if you force it. Paint dries how it wants. Making teaches humility and patience, and it gives you proof, physical proof, that you were here and you changed something, even if it's just dinner. I think we all need at least one project that is slow and unnecessary and entirely ours. Unnecessary is important. Not everything has to optimize or monetize or scale. Some things can just be delightful.

Under all of this is uncertainty, humming like a refrigerator in the background of modern life. We don't know what's coming — in our own lives, let alone in the world. Climate, politics, technology, health, love: so much feels volatile and unresolved. It's tempting to respond by either numbing out or trying to control everything. But there's a third option, older and wiser: learn to live well inside the not-knowing. Farmers have always known this. Artists know it. Anyone who has raised a child or planted a garden or loved anyone knows it. You do the work, you pay attention, you adjust, and you release your grip on the outcome. Uncertainty isn't a bug to be fixed; it's the condition that makes curiosity, courage, and kindness matter. If we knew how everything would turn out, we wouldn't need faith or improvisation or hope. The open ending is what lets us be authors, not just readers, of our lives.

Language itself feels like a miracle I never get over. That we can make small noises with our mouths, or little marks on a page or screen, and transfer an image from one mind to another — it's absurd and wonderful. I can write "the smell of rain on hot pavement in July" and somewhere inside you, a memory stirs, even if your July was decades ago and thousands of miles from mine. Words fail constantly, of course. They flatten. They misunderstand. But they also reach. Every conversation, every letter, every late-night voice memo is an attempt to bridge the solitude of being a single consciousness in a single body. Sometimes the bridge holds. Someone says exactly what you needed, or you find the sentence that finally says what you meant. Those moments feel like grace.

So if I had a thousand words — and I suppose I just used them — I would spend them on this reminder: notice more. Look longer. Ask better questions. Make something small and useless and lovely. Take the train. Sit in the library until the light changes. Let the morning be a draft you revise with kindness. The world is not just content to be consumed; it's a place to be inhabited, witnessed, tended. We are only here briefly, each of us a short, bright attention moving through an enormous mystery. What a shame it would be to sleepwalk through it. What a joy it is, when we remember, to wake up in the middle of our own lives and realize we get to pay attention on purpose — and in doing so, to make a life that feels, sentence by sentence, like our own.
